Differentiation

Units 7–8 · 14 methods

Part III (PDF) All parts

Units 7–8: limits, the rules of differentiation, and what a derivative is for, from tangents and the existence of roots to extreme values, sketches, optimisation and iterative methods. Most problems start by finding a derivative; the question decides what to do with it.

Unit 7 · Differentiation I: limits and the rules

The notes · The problems · Name the method

Seven methods: two for limits, one that finds a derivative as a limit, and four that differentiate. Which of the four depends on how the function is given. A tangent line, a velocity, a higher derivative and a sensitivity are each one step after the rules, and are variants of Method 7.4.

Which method?

What you see What to do
one formula on both sides of aaa, and substituting gives a number 7.1: that number is the limit
00\tfrac0000​, and top and bottom share a factor 7.1: factor and cancel
00\tfrac0000​ with a square root, or with 1−cos⁡x1-\cos x1−cosx 7.1: multiply by the conjugate
00\tfrac0000​ with the sine of something small 7.1: rewrite to sin⁡uu\tfrac{\sin u}{u}usinu​
(a nonzero number)/0/0/0 7.1: one-sided limits; an asymptote
x→∞x\to\inftyx→∞ with a rational function, or a difference with a root 7.1: conjugate first for a root; divide by the highest power
a join in a piecewise function 7.2: one-sided limits at the join
“from first principles” 7.3: the difference quotient
a product or quotient of two factors, a function of a function 7.4: name uuu and vvv, or outer and inner
yyy tangled with xxx in an equation 7.5: implicit differentiation
xxx and yyy both given in terms of ttt 7.6: parametric differentiation
the variable in both a base and an exponent; a product or quotient of three or more factors 7.7: take logarithms first

7.1 Evaluating a limit

Problem. Find lim⁡x→af(x)\lim_{x\to a}f(x)limx→a​f(x), the one-sided limits at aaa, or lim⁡x→∞f(x)\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)limx→∞​f(x), and the asymptotes they give.

Method

  1. If fff is one formula on both sides of aaa, substitute x=ax=ax=a into it. If the result is a number, that is the limit. At the join of a piecewise function, find the two one-sided limits instead (Method 7.2, step 2).

  2. If it is 00\tfrac0000​, simplify for x≠ax\ne ax=a: factor and cancel the common factor; multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of a root (for 1−cos⁡x1-\cos x1−cosx, by 1+cos⁡x1+\cos x1+cosx, then 1−cos⁡2x=sin⁡2x1-\cos^2x=\sin^2x1−cos2x=sin2x); or rewrite to sin⁡uu\dfrac{\sin u}{u}usinu​ with u→0u\to0u→0, using lim⁡u→0sin⁡uu=1\lim_{u\to0}\dfrac{\sin u}{u}=1limu→0​usinu​=1.

  3. Substitute into the simplified form, and state the limit.

  4. If it is (a nonzero number)/0/0/0, find the limits from below and from above, x→a−x\to a^-x→a− and x→a+x\to a^+x→a+, from the signs of the top and the bottom. An infinite one gives the vertical asymptote x=ax=ax=a. The limit exists only when the two one-sided limits exist and agree.

  5. For x→∞x\to\inftyx→∞, divide the top and the bottom by the highest power of xxx in the denominator. Each 1/xk1/x^k1/xk tends to 000: write the (⋅)−0(⋅)+0\dfrac{(\cdot)-0}{(\cdot)+0}(⋅)+0(⋅)−0​ line. For a difference with a root, multiply and divide by its conjugate first, as in step 2.

  6. If the limit is a number LLL, state it and the horizontal asymptote y=Ly=Ly=L. For a rational function the same LLL holds as x→−∞x\to-\inftyx→−∞; for any other function, check that direction separately. If a power of xxx is left on the top, the limit is infinite and there is no horizontal asymptote.

Example (a) For f(x)=2x2−5x+3x2−xf(x)=\dfrac{2x^2-5x+3}{x^2-x}f(x)=x2−x2x2−5x+3​, find the limits of fff as x→1x\to1x→1, as x→0±x\to0^{\pm}x→0± and as x→∞x\to\inftyx→∞, and the asymptotes. 7.2 Continuity and differentiability at a join

Problem. Decide whether a function, often defined piecewise, is continuous or differentiable at a point; choose constants that make it so.

Method

  1. Find f(a)f(a)f(a), from the piece that includes x=ax=ax=a.

  2. Find lim⁡x→af(x)\lim_{x\to a}f(x)limx→a​f(x). At a join, find the two one-sided limits, each from the piece on its own side.

  3. fff is continuous at aaa when the limit exists and equals f(a)f(a)f(a). Equate them; with an unknown constant, this is an equation for it.

  4. For differentiability, impose continuity first: a function differentiable at aaa is continuous there.

  5. Find the one-sided limits of the difference quotient f(a+δx)−f(a)δx\dfrac{f(a+\delta x)-f(a)}{\delta x}δxf(a+δx)−f(a)​ as δx→0−\delta x\to0^-δx→0− and as δx→0+\delta x\to0^+δx→0+, each side from its own piece.

  6. fff is differentiable at aaa exactly when they are finite and agree, and f′(a)f'(a)f′(a) is the common value. If they differ, the graph has a corner; if either is infinite, there is no derivative.

Example (a) Find aaa and bbb so that f(x)={x2+1,x≤1ax+b,x>1f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2+1,&x\le1\\ \dfrac ax+b,&x>1\end{cases}f(x)={x2+1,xa​+b,​x≤1x>1​ is differentiable at x=1x=1x=1. (b) Show that h(x)={x2,x≤0sin⁡x,x>0h(x)=\begin{cases}x^2,&x\le0\\ \sin x,&x>0\end{cases}h(x)={x2,sinx,​x≤0x>0​ is continuous but not differentiable at 000.

(a) f(1)=2f(1)=2f(1)=2, from the left piece, and the one-sided limits are 222 from below and a+ba+ba+b from above. Continuity needs a+b=2a+b=2a+b=2. With b=2−ab=2-ab=2−a the difference quotients are (1+δx)2+1−2δx=2+δx→δx→0−2,1δx(a1+δx−a)=−a1+δx→δx→0+−a.\begin{align*} \frac{(1+\delta x)^2+1-2}{\delta x}&=2+\delta x \xrightarrow[\delta x\to0^-]{}2,\\ \frac{1}{\delta x}\Bigl(\frac{a}{1+\delta x}-a\Bigr)&=\frac{-a}{1+\delta x} \xrightarrow[\delta x\to0^+]{}-a . \end{align*}δx(1+δx)2+1−2​δx1​(1+δxa​−a)​=2+δxδx→0−​2,=1+δx−a​δx→0+​−a.​ They agree only if −a=2-a=2−a=2, and then b=2−ab=2-ab=2−a: a=−2, b=4\boxed{a=-2,\ b=4}a=−2, b=4​.

(b) h(0)=0h(0)=0h(0)=0, and the one-sided limits are 02=00^2=002=0 and sin⁡0=0\sin0=0sin0=0: hhh is continuous at 000. The difference quotients are (δx)2δx=δx→0\dfrac{(\delta x)^2}{\delta x}=\delta x\to0δx(δx)2​=δx→0 from below and sin⁡δxδx→1\dfrac{\sin\delta x}{\delta x}\to1δxsinδx​→1 from above. They differ, so hhh is not differentiable at 000: its graph has a corner there.

Check. In (a) the right piece is 4−2x4-\tfrac2x4−x2​. As x→1+x\to1^+x→1+ its value tends to 222 and its slope 2x2\tfrac2{x^2}x22​ to 222, the same as the value and the slope 2x=22x=22x=2 of x2+1x^2+1x2+1 at 111. In (b) the slopes of the two pieces at 000 are 2x=02x=02x=0 and cos⁡x=1\cos x=1cosx=1: they differ, so there is a corner.

Pitfalls

  • Matching the slopes and skipping continuity. With a=−2a=-2a=−2 and b=0b=0b=0 the slopes match, but fff jumps from 222 to −2-2−2, so it is not even continuous.

  • Taking f(a)f(a)f(a) from the wrong piece. Read ≤\le≤ and <<< in the definition.

  • Concluding from continuity that fff is differentiable. The function hhh in (b) is continuous and has a corner.

7.3 Differentiating from first principles

Problem. Find f′(x)f'(x)f′(x) from the definition f′(x)=lim⁡δx→0f(x+δx)−f(x)δxf'(x)=\lim_{\delta x\to0}\dfrac{f(x+\delta x)-f(x)}{\delta x}f′(x)=limδx→0​δxf(x+δx)−f(x)​, without the rules.

Method

  1. Write the difference quotient f(x+δx)−f(x)δx\dfrac{f(x+\delta x)-f(x)}{\delta x}δxf(x+δx)−f(x)​.

  2. Simplify the numerator: expand a power; bring fractions to a common denominator; for a root, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.

  3. Every term of the numerator now carries a factor δx\delta xδx. Cancel it with the δx\delta xδx below.

  4. Let δx→0\delta x\to0δx→0 in what is left: “letting δx→0\delta x\to0δx→0 leaves f′(x)=…f'(x)=\dotsf′(x)=…”.

Example Differentiate from first principles (a) f(x)=1x2f(x)=\dfrac1{x^2}f(x)=x21​ and (b) g(x)=x2+4g(x)=\sqrt{x^2+4}g(x)=x2+4​.

(a) Bring the two fractions to the denominator x2(x+δx)2x^2(x+\delta x)^2x2(x+δx)2 and expand the top: f(x+δx)−f(x)δx=x2−(x+δx)2δx x2(x+δx)2=−2x δx−(δx)2δx x2(x+δx)2=−(2x+δx)x2(x+δx)2.\begin{align*} \frac{f(x+\delta x)-f(x)}{\delta x} &=\frac{x^2-(x+\delta x)^2}{\delta x\,x^2(x+\delta x)^2}\\ &=\frac{-2x\,\delta x-(\delta x)^2}{\delta x\,x^2(x+\delta x)^2}\\ &=\frac{-(2x+\delta x)}{x^2(x+\delta x)^2}. \end{align*}δxf(x+δx)−f(x)​​=δxx2(x+δx)2x2−(x+δx)2​=δxx2(x+δx)2−2xδx−(δx)2​=x2(x+δx)2−(2x+δx)​.​ Letting δx→0\delta x\to0δx→0 leaves f′(x)=−2xx4f'(x)=\dfrac{-2x}{x^4}f′(x)=x4−2x​, so f′(x)=−2x3\boxed{f'(x)=-\dfrac{2}{x^3}}f′(x)=−x32​​.

(b) Multiply top and bottom by (x+δx)2+4+x2+4\sqrt{(x+\delta x)^2+4}+\sqrt{x^2+4}(x+δx)2+4​+x2+4​. The top becomes (x+δx)2+4−(x2+4)=2x δx+(δx)2(x+\delta x)^2+4-(x^2+4)=2x\,\delta x+(\delta x)^2(x+δx)2+4−(x2+4)=2xδx+(δx)2, so g(x+δx)−g(x)δx=2x+δx(x+δx)2+4+x2+4.\frac{g(x+\delta x)-g(x)}{\delta x} =\frac{2x+\delta x}{\sqrt{(x+\delta x)^2+4}+\sqrt{x^2+4}} .δxg(x+δx)−g(x)​=(x+δx)2+4​+x2+4​2x+δx​. Letting δx→0\delta x\to0δx→0 leaves 2x2x2+4\dfrac{2x}{2\sqrt{x^2+4}}2x2+4​2x​, so g′(x)=xx2+4\boxed{g'(x)=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}}g′(x)=x2+4​x​​.

Check. The rules give the same:  d dx x−2=−2x−3\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\,x^{-2}=-2x^{-3}dxd​x−2=−2x−3, and the chain rule gives 12(x2+4)−1/2⋅2x\tfrac12(x^2+4)^{-1/2}\cdot2x21​(x2+4)−1/2⋅2x.

Pitfalls

  • Expanding (x+δx)2(x+\delta x)^2(x+δx)2 as x2+(δx)2x^2+(\delta x)^2x2+(δx)2. The cross term 2x δx2x\,\delta x2xδx is the one that survives.

  • Writing f(x)+δxf(x)+\delta xf(x)+δx for f(x+δx)f(x+\delta x)f(x+δx). In (b), g(x+δx)=(x+δx)2+4g(x+\delta x)=\sqrt{(x+\delta x)^2+4}g(x+δx)=(x+δx)2+4​, not x2+4+δx\sqrt{x^2+4}+\delta xx2+4​+δx.

7.4 Choosing between the product, quotient and chain rules

Problem. Differentiate a function built from standard functions by products, quotients and composition, and simplify the result.

Method

  1. Find the last operation in the formula: a product uvuvuv, a quotient u/vu/vu/v, or a function of a function f(g(x))f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)f(g(x)). It decides the rule.

  2. Name uuu and vvv; or the outer function f(u)f(u)f(u) and the inner u=g(x)u=g(x)u=g(x).

  3. Find u′u'u′ and v′v'v′ from the standard derivatives, using the chain rule inside when uuu or vvv is itself a function of a function.

  4. Apply the rule: (uv)′=u′v+uv′(uv)'=u'v+uv'(uv)′=u′v+uv′; (uv)′=u′v−uv′v2\bigl(\tfrac uv\bigr)'=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}(vu​)′=v2u′v−uv′​;  dy dx= dy du⋅ du dx\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}u}\cdot\frac{\,\mathrm{d}u}{\,\mathrm{d}x}dxdy​=dudy​⋅dxdu​.

  5. Simplify: clear any fraction inside the numerator, and take out the common factor or power.

Variants. A tangent line at x=ax=ax=a: find f(a)f(a)f(a) and f′(a)f'(a)f′(a), write the point–slope form y−f(a)=f′(a)(x−a)y-f(a)=f'(a)(x-a)y−f(a)=f′(a)(x−a), and rearrange to y=mx+cy=mx+cy=mx+c. Motion along a line: the velocity is v=s˙v=\dot sv=s˙ and the acceleration a=s¨a=\ddot sa=s¨, with units; the body is at rest where v=0v=0v=0, found by factoring, and the sign of vvv gives the direction. Higher derivatives: differentiate again and again, listing f′f'f′, f′′f''f′′, …; for a polynomial, stop at the first 000. A sensitivity: evaluate  dL dw\frac{\,\mathrm{d}L}{\,\mathrm{d}w}dwdL​ at the current www; a small step that reduces LLL moves www against the sign of  dL dw\frac{\,\mathrm{d}L}{\,\mathrm{d}w}dwdL​.

Example (a) Differentiate y=x5−xy=x\sqrt{5-x}y=x5−x​, and find the tangent line at x=4x=4x=4. (b) Differentiate y=cos⁡x1+sin⁡xy=\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}y=1+sinxcosx​.

(a) A product: u=xu=xu=x and v=(5−x)1/2v=(5-x)^{1/2}v=(5−x)1/2. Then u′=1u'=1u′=1, and by the chain rule, with inner 5−x5-x5−x of derivative −1-1−1, v′=12(5−x)−1/2⋅(−1)v'=\tfrac12(5-x)^{-1/2}\cdot(-1)v′=21​(5−x)−1/2⋅(−1). So  dy dx=5−x−x25−x.\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}=\sqrt{5-x}-\frac{x}{2\sqrt{5-x}} .dxdy​=5−x​−25−x​x​. Put both terms over the common denominator 25−x2\sqrt{5-x}25−x​; the top is 2(5−x)−x2(5-x)-x2(5−x)−x:  dy dx=10−3x25−x\boxed{\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{10-3x}{2\sqrt{5-x}}}dxdy​=25−x​10−3x​​ At x=4x=4x=4: y=4⋅1=4y=4\cdot1=4y=4⋅1=4 and  dy dx=−22=−1\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}=\tfrac{-2}{2}=-1dxdy​=2−2​=−1. The point–slope form y−4=−(x−4)y-4=-(x-4)y−4=−(x−4) gives the tangent y=8−x\boxed{y=8-x}y=8−x​.

(b) A quotient: u=cos⁡xu=\cos xu=cosx and v=1+sin⁡xv=1+\sin xv=1+sinx, with u′=−sin⁡xu'=-\sin xu′=−sinx and v′=cos⁡xv'=\cos xv′=cosx.  dy dx=−sin⁡x (1+sin⁡x)−cos⁡2x(1+sin⁡x)2=−sin⁡x−(sin⁡2x+cos⁡2x)(1+sin⁡x)2=−(1+sin⁡x)(1+sin⁡x)2,\begin{align*} \frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{-\sin x\,(1+\sin x)-\cos^2x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\ &=\frac{-\sin x-(\sin^2x+\cos^2x)}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\ &=\frac{-(1+\sin x)}{(1+\sin x)^2}, \end{align*}dxdy​​=(1+sinx)2−sinx(1+sinx)−cos2x​=(1+sinx)2−sinx−(sin2x+cos2x)​=(1+sinx)2−(1+sinx)​,​ so  dy dx=−11+sin⁡x\boxed{\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}=-\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}}dxdy​=−1+sinx1​​.

7.5 Implicit differentiation

Problem. A curve is given by an equation in xxx and yyy. Find the slope y′= dy dxy'=\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}y′=dxdy​, its value at a point, and the second derivative y′′y''y′′.

Method

  1. Differentiate both sides with respect to xxx, treating yyy as a function of xxx. By the chain rule  d dx g(y)=g′(y) y′\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\,g(y)=g'(y)\,y'dxd​g(y)=g′(y)y′; a product such as xyxyxy needs the product rule, y+xy′y+xy'y+xy′.

  2. Collect the terms in y′y'y′ on one side.

  3. Solve for y′y'y′, where its coefficient is not zero.

  4. Evaluate at the point, having checked that the point lies on the curve.

  5. For y′′y''y′′, differentiate the relation from step 1 once more, substitute the values of xxx, yyy and y′y'y′, and solve for y′′y''y′′.

The tangent is horizontal where  dy/ dt=0\,\mathrm{d}y/\,\mathrm{d}t=0dy/dt=0 and  dx/ dt≠0\,\mathrm{d}x/\,\mathrm{d}t\ne0dx/dt=0, and vertical where  dx/ dt=0\,\mathrm{d}x/\,\mathrm{d}t=0dx/dt=0 and  dy/ dt≠0\,\mathrm{d}y/\,\mathrm{d}t\ne0dy/dt=0. 7.7 Logarithmic differentiation

Problem. Differentiate a function with the variable in both a base and an exponent, or a product or quotient of many factors.

Method

  1. Take ln⁡∣ ⋅ ∣\ln\left|\,\cdot\,\right|ln∣⋅∣ of both sides. Where y>0y>0y>0 throughout, as for xxx^xxx with x>0x>0x>0, plain ln⁡\lnln will do; say so.

  2. Simplify with the log laws: a product becomes a sum, a quotient a difference, and a power a multiplier.

  3. Differentiate both sides with respect to xxx. The left side gives 1y dy dx\dfrac1y\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}y1​dxdy​ by the chain rule; the right side goes term by term.

  4. Multiply back by yyy, written in terms of xxx, and state where the result holds: away from the zeros of the factors. At a zero of a power factor, such as x=0x=0x=0 for x3x^3x3, yyy is still defined: find y′y'y′ there by the product rule instead.

(a) For x>0x>0x>0, y>0y>0y>0, so ln⁡y=x ln⁡x\ln y=\sqrt x\,\ln xlny=x​lnx. Differentiate, by the product rule on the right: 1y dy dx=ln⁡x2x+x⋅1x=ln⁡x+22x.\frac1y\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{\ln x}{2\sqrt x}+\sqrt x\cdot\frac1x =\frac{\ln x+2}{2\sqrt x} .y1​dxdy​=2x​lnx​+x​⋅x1​=2x​lnx+2​. Multiply back by yyy:  dy dx=xx ln⁡x+22x\boxed{\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}=x^{\sqrt x}\,\frac{\ln x+2}{2\sqrt x}}dxdy​=xx​2x​lnx+2​​ At x=4x=4x=4: y=42=16y=4^2=16y=42=16, so  dy dx=16⋅ln⁡4+24=8(1+ln⁡2)\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}=16\cdot\dfrac{\ln4+2}{4}=\boxed{8(1+\ln2)}dxdy​=16⋅4ln4+2​=8(1+ln2)​.

(b) For x>−1x>-1x>−1, x≠0x\ne0x=0, x≠2x\ne2x=2: ln⁡∣y∣=3ln⁡∣x∣+12ln⁡(x+1)−2ln⁡∣x−2∣\ln\left|y\right|=3\ln\left|x\right|+\tfrac12\ln(x+1)-2\ln\left|x-2\right|ln∣y∣=3ln∣x∣+21​ln(x+1)−2ln∣x−2∣. At x=0x=0x=0, where y=0y=0y=0, the product rule on x3⋅x+1(x−2)2x^3\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{x+1}}{(x-2)^2}x3⋅(x−2)2x+1​​ gives two terms, each with a factor x2x^2x2, so y′(0)=0y'(0)=0y′(0)=0.

Unit 8 · Differentiation II: applications

The notes · The problems · Name the method

Seven methods. Nearly every problem starts by computing f′f'f′, so what decides the method is what the question asks for. The derivative of an inverse function is a variant of Method 8.2.

Which method?

The question asks for Method
the tangent or the normal at a point 8.1
“show that the equation has a root in [a,b][a,b][a,b]” 8.2, a sign change (IVT)
“… and it has exactly one root” 8.2, add the sign of f′f'f′
a value ccc with f′(c)f'(c)f′(c) equal to a secant slope; a bound on ∣f(b)−f(a)∣\left|f(b)-f(a)\right|∣f(b)−f(a)∣ 8.2, the mean value theorem
the slope of f−1f^{-1}f−1 at a point 8.2, variant: 1/f′(a)1/f'(a)1/f′(a)
a limit of the form 00\tfrac0000​ or ∞∞\tfrac\infty\infty∞∞​ 8.3, l’Hôpital’s rule
a limit of the form 0⋅∞0\cdot\infty0⋅∞ or ∞−∞\infty-\infty∞−∞ 8.3, rewrite as a quotient first
a local maximum or minimum; “classify” 8.4, the derivative tests

8.1 Tangent and normal

Problem. Find the tangent line and the normal line to the curve y=f(x)y=f(x)y=f(x) at the point where x=ax=ax=a, or where the tangent has a given slope.

Method

  1. Compute f(a)f(a)f(a) and f′(a)f'(a)f′(a): differentiate first, then put x=ax=ax=a. If the point is given by its slope instead (a horizontal tangent has slope 000), first solve f′(a)=f'(a)=f′(a)= that slope for aaa, keeping solutions in the domain.

  2. Tangent: y=f(a)+f′(a) (x−a)y=f(a)+f'(a)\,(x-a)y=f(a)+f′(a)(x−a). Simplify it to the form y=mx+cy=mx+cy=mx+c.

  3. Normal: its slope is −1/f′(a)-1/f'(a)−1/f′(a), so y=f(a)−1f′(a) (x−a)y=f(a)-\dfrac{1}{f'(a)}\,(x-a)y=f(a)−f′(a)1​(x−a). If f′(a)=0f'(a)=0f′(a)=0, the tangent is the horizontal line y=f(a)y=f(a)y=f(a) and the normal is the vertical line x=ax=ax=a.

  4. Check that the two slopes multiply to −1-1−1 (when f′(a)≠0f'(a)\ne0f′(a)=0), and that both lines pass through (a,f(a))\bigl(a,f(a)\bigr)(a,f(a)).

Example For the curve y=xx+3y=x\sqrt{x+3}y=xx+3​, find (a) the tangent and the normal at the point where x=1x=1x=1, and (b) the tangent and the normal at the point where the tangent is horizontal.

By the product rule, f′(x)=x+3+x2x+3=3x+62x+3.f'(x)=\sqrt{x+3}+\frac{x}{2\sqrt{x+3}}=\frac{3x+6}{2\sqrt{x+3}} .f′(x)=x+3​+2x+3​x​=2x+3​3x+6​. (a) f(1)=1⋅4=2f(1)=1\cdot\sqrt4=2f(1)=1⋅4​=2 and f′(1)=2+14=94f'(1)=2+\tfrac14=\tfrac94f′(1)=2+41​=49​. The tangent is y=2+94(x−1)⟹y=94x−14y=2+\tfrac94(x-1) \quad\allowbreak \Longrightarrow\quad\allowbreak \boxed{y=\tfrac94x-\tfrac14}y=2+49​(x−1)⟹y=49​x−41​​ The normal has slope −1/94=−49-1\big/\tfrac94=-\tfrac49−1/49​=−94​: y=2−49(x−1)⟹y=−49x+229y=2-\tfrac49(x-1) \quad\allowbreak \Longrightarrow\quad\allowbreak \boxed{y=-\tfrac49x+\tfrac{22}9}y=2−94​(x−1)⟹y=−94​x+922​​ (b) f′(x)=0f'(x)=0f′(x)=0 where 3x+6=03x+6=03x+6=0, that is at x=−2x=-2x=−2, which is in the domain x≥−3x\ge-3x≥−3. There f(−2)=−21=−2f(-2)=-2\sqrt1=-2f(−2)=−21​=−2. The tangent is horizontal, so the normal is vertical: tangent y=−2,normal x=−2\boxed{\text{tangent } y=-2,\quad \text{normal } x=-2}tangent y=−2,normal x=−2​

Check. (a) The slopes multiply to 94⋅(−49)=−1\tfrac94\cdot\bigl(-\tfrac49\bigr)=-149​⋅(−94​)=−1, and both lines pass through (1,2)(1,2)(1,2): 94−14=2\tfrac94-\tfrac14=249​−41​=2 and −49+229=2-\tfrac49+\tfrac{22}9=2−94​+922​=2. The slope itself: (f(1.001)−f(1))/0.001≈2.2502\bigl(f(1.001)-f(1)\bigr)/0.001\approx2.2502(f(1.001)−f(1))/0.001≈2.2502, close to 94\tfrac9449​. (b) y=−2y=-2y=−2 and x=−2x=-2x=−2 both pass through (−2,−2)=(−2,f(−2))(-2,-2)=\bigl(-2,f(-2)\bigr)(−2,−2)=(−2,f(−2)).

Pitfalls

  • Leaving xxx in the slope. The tangent’s slope is the number f′(1)=94f'(1)=\tfrac94f′(1)=49​, not the function f′(x)f'(x)f′(x).

8.2 A root exists and is unique (IVT and monotonicity); the mean value theorem

Problem. Show that an equation has a root in a given interval, and that it has no other; find the point ccc that the mean value theorem promises, or use the theorem to bound a difference.

Method

  1. For a root: write the equation as f(x)=0f(x)=0f(x)=0, with everything on one side.

  2. State that fff is continuous on [a,b][a,b][a,b]: polynomials, ex\mathrm{e}^xex, ln⁡x\ln xlnx, sin⁡x\sin xsinx, cos⁡x\cos xcosx and their sums, products, quotients and compositions are continuous wherever they are defined, so check that fff is defined at every point of [a,b][a,b][a,b].

  3. Evaluate f(a)f(a)f(a) and f(b)f(b)f(b), and show that they have opposite signs.

  4. Conclude by the intermediate value theorem: f(c)=0f(c)=0f(c)=0 for some c∈(a,b)c\in(a,b)c∈(a,b).

  5. Uniqueness: show that f′>0f'>0f′>0 (or f′<0f'<0f′<0) on the whole domain of fff, which must be an interval, usually R\mathbb{R}R. By the monotonicity corollary, which holds on an interval, fff is then strictly monotone, so it takes the value 000 at most once.

  6. Mean value theorem (start here for a secant slope or a bound): check that fff is continuous on [a,b][a,b][a,b] and differentiable on (a,b)(a,b)(a,b). Compute the secant slope f(b)−f(a)b−a\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}b−af(b)−f(a)​, solve f′(c)=f'(c)=f′(c)= slope, and keep only the solutions with c∈(a,b)c\in(a,b)c∈(a,b).

Variants. A bound: apply the mean value theorem between the two points, f(b)−f(a)=f′(c) (b−a)f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)\,(b-a)f(b)−f(a)=f′(c)(b−a), and replace ∣f′(c)∣\left|f'(c)\right|∣f′(c)∣ by the largest value ∣f′∣\left|f'\right|∣f′∣ takes between the two points. The derivative of an inverse: once f′>0f'>0f′>0 (or f′<0f'<0f′<0) shows that fff is one-to-one, (f−1)′(b)=1/f′(a)(f^{-1})'(b)=1/f'(a)(f−1)′(b)=1/f′(a), where aaa solves f(a)=bf(a)=bf(a)=b (usually by inspection) and f′(a)≠0f'(a)\ne0f′(a)=0. No formula for f−1f^{-1}f−1 is needed.

Example (a) Show that ex+x=2\mathrm{e}^x+x=2ex+x=2 has exactly one real solution, and that it lies in (0,1)(0,1)(0,1). (b) Find the value of ccc that the mean value theorem gives for f(x)=1xf(x)=\dfrac1xf(x)=x1​ on [1,4][1,4][1,4].

(a) Write the equation as g(x)=ex+x−2=0g(x)=\mathrm{e}^x+x-2=0g(x)=ex+x−2=0. The function ggg, an exponential plus a polynomial, is continuous on R\mathbb{R}R, and g(0)=1+0−2=−1<0,g(1)=e−1>0.g(0)=1+0-2=-1<0,\qquad\allowbreak g(1)=\mathrm{e}-1>0 .g(0)=1+0−2=−1<0,g(1)=e−1>0. By the intermediate value theorem, g(c)=0g(c)=0g(c)=0 for some c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1)c∈(0,1). And g′(x)=ex+1>0g'(x)=\mathrm{e}^x+1>0g′(x)=ex+1>0 for every xxx, so ggg is strictly increasing and has at most one zero. So there is exactly one root, in (0,1)\boxed{\text{exactly one root, in }(0,1)}exactly one root, in (0,1)​.

(b) f(x)=1/xf(x)=1/xf(x)=1/x is continuous on [1,4][1,4][1,4] and differentiable on (1,4)(1,4)(1,4), since 000 is not in the interval. The secant slope is f(4)−f(1)4−1=14−13=−14.\frac{f(4)-f(1)}{4-1}=\frac{\tfrac14-1}{3}=-\frac14 .4−1f(4)−f(1)​=341​−1​=−41​. Solve f′(c)=−1c2=−14f'(c)=-\dfrac1{c^2}=-\dfrac14f′(c)=−c21​=−41​: c2=4c^2=4c2=4, so c=±2c=\pm2c=±2. Only one of them lies in (1,4)(1,4)(1,4): c=2\boxed{c=2}c=2​.

Check. (a) One more sign: g(12)=e−32≈0.15>0g(\tfrac12)=\sqrt\mathrm{e}-\tfrac32\approx0.15>0g(21​)=e​−23​≈0.15>0, so the root is in fact in (0,12)(0,\tfrac12)(0,21​), and Method 8.7 finds it there. (b) f′(2)=−14f'(2)=-\tfrac14f′(2)=−41​, the slope of the secant.

Pitfalls

  • Stopping at the sign change when “exactly one” is asked. The intermediate value theorem gives at least one root, never uniqueness.

  • Skipping the continuity check. On [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] the function 1/x1/x1/x has f(−1)<0<f(1)f(-1)<0<f(1)f(−1)<0<f(1) but no root. Its secant slope is 111 while f′<0f'<0f′<0 everywhere, so there is no mean-value point either: 1/x1/x1/x is not defined at 000, so it is not continuous on [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1].

  • Keeping c=−2c=-2c=−2. The theorem promises a point strictly inside (a,b)(a,b)(a,b).

8.3 l’Hôpital’s rule

Problem. Evaluate a limit of an indeterminate form: 00\tfrac0000​, ∞∞\tfrac\infty\infty∞∞​, 0⋅∞0\cdot\infty0⋅∞ or ∞−∞\infty-\infty∞−∞.

Method

  1. Substitute the limit point and name the form. If it is not indeterminate, the rule does not apply: a finite value is the answer, and a non-zero number over 000 means an infinite limit, or none if the two sides differ (Unit 7).

  2. Rewrite 0⋅∞0\cdot\infty0⋅∞ as a quotient, fg=f1/gfg=\dfrac{f}{1/g}fg=1/gf​, sending down a factor ggg whose reciprocal is simple (for g=xg=xg=x, 1/x1/x1/x); if the new quotient is no simpler, send down the other factor. Rewrite a difference of fractions over a common denominator; with no fractions, factor out the larger term: x−ln⁡x=x(1−ln⁡xx)x-\ln x=x\bigl(1-\tfrac{\ln x}{x}\bigr)x−lnx=x(1−xlnx​). Each leaves a 00\tfrac0000​ or ∞∞\tfrac\infty\infty∞∞​ quotient.

  3. Apply the rule: differentiate the numerator and the denominator separately, and mark the step =H\overset{\mathrm H}{=}=H.

  4. Simplify, and check the form again before every repeat. Stop using the rule as soon as the form is no longer indeterminate.

  5. Evaluate, as in step 1.

Example Evaluate (a) lim⁡x→∞x(e2/x−1)\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}x\bigl(\mathrm{e}^{2/x}-1\bigr)x→∞lim​x(e2/x−1) and (b) lim⁡x→0(1x−1ex−1)\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\Bigl(\frac1x-\frac1{\mathrm{e}^x-1}\Bigr)x→0lim​(x1​−ex−11​).

(a) As x→∞x\to\inftyx→∞, e2/x→1\mathrm{e}^{2/x}\to1e2/x→1, so the form is ∞⋅0\infty\cdot0∞⋅0. Rewrite it as e2/x−11/x\dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{2/x}-1}{1/x}1/xe2/x−1​, a 00\tfrac0000​ form. By the chain rule the top differentiates to −2x2e2/x-\tfrac2{x^2}\mathrm{e}^{2/x}−x22​e2/x and the bottom to −1x2-\tfrac1{x^2}−x21​, so lim⁡x→∞e2/x−11/x=Hlim⁡x→∞2e2/x=2.\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\mathrm{e}^{2/x}-1}{1/x} \overset{\mathrm H}{=}\lim_{x\to\infty}2\mathrm{e}^{2/x}=\boxed{2} .x→∞lim​1/xe2/x−1​=Hx→∞lim​2e2/x=2​. (b) The form is ∞−∞\infty-\infty∞−∞. Over the common denominator x(ex−1)x(\mathrm{e}^x-1)x(ex−1), 1x−1ex−1=ex−1−xx(ex−1),\frac1x-\frac1{\mathrm{e}^x-1}=\frac{\mathrm{e}^x-1-x}{x(\mathrm{e}^x-1)} ,x1​−ex−11​=x(ex−1)ex−1−x​, a 00\tfrac0000​ form. Then lim⁡x→0ex−1−xx(ex−1)=Hlim⁡x→0ex−1ex−1+xex,\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\mathrm{e}^x-1-x}{x(\mathrm{e}^x-1)} \overset{\mathrm H}{=}\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\mathrm{e}^x-1}{\mathrm{e}^x-1+x\mathrm{e}^x} ,x→0lim​x(ex−1)ex−1−x​=Hx→0lim​ex−1+xexex−1​, which is still 00\tfrac0000​, so apply the rule again: lim⁡x→0ex−1ex−1+xex=Hlim⁡x→0ex2ex+xex=12.\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\mathrm{e}^x-1}{\mathrm{e}^x-1+x\mathrm{e}^x} \overset{\mathrm H}{=}\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\mathrm{e}^x}{2\mathrm{e}^x+x\mathrm{e}^x}=\boxed{\tfrac12} .x→0lim​ex−1+xexex−1​=Hx→0lim​2ex+xexex​=21​​.

Check. Numerically: at x=1000x=1000x=1000 the expression in (a) is 2.00202.00202.0020, and at x=0.01x=0.01x=0.01 the one in (b) is 0.49920.49920.4992.

Pitfalls

  • Using the rule once too often. In (b) the last quotient tends to 12\tfrac1221​, not 00\tfrac0000​; one more application would give 13\tfrac1331​.

  • Applying the rule to 0⋅∞0\cdot\infty0⋅∞ or ∞−∞\infty-\infty∞−∞ before rewriting it as a single quotient.

  • Differentiating f/gf/gf/g by the quotient rule. The rule differentiates the top and the bottom separately.

8.4 Classifying critical points; the closed-interval method

Problem. Find the critical points of fff and classify each as a local maximum, a local minimum or neither; find the absolute maximum and minimum of a continuous fff on a closed interval [a,b][a,b][a,b].

Method

  1. Find f′f'f′ and factor it. The critical points are the solutions of f′(x)=0f'(x)=0f′(x)=0 in the domain, together with any point of the domain where f′f'f′ does not exist.

  2. Classify each stationary point by the second-derivative test where it is quick: f′′(c)>0f''(c)>0f′′(c)>0 gives a local minimum, f′′(c)<0f''(c)<0f′′(c)<0 a local maximum.

  3. If f′′(c)=0f''(c)=0f′′(c)=0, or f′(c)f'(c)f′(c) does not exist, use the first-derivative test instead: the sign of f′f'f′ on each side of ccc. From +++ to −-− is a maximum, from −-− to +++ a minimum, and the same strict sign on both sides is neither. If f′=0f'=0f′=0 on one side, as for (ReLU⁡(x))2\bigl(\operatorname{ReLU}(x)\bigr)^2(ReLU(x))2 at 000, no pattern applies: compare f(x)f(x)f(x) with f(c)f(c)f(c) on both sides.

  4. State each result as a point: “local maximum at (c,f(c))\bigl(c,f(c)\bigr)(c,f(c))”, or neither.

  5. On a closed interval: keep the critical points inside [a,b][a,b][a,b], and evaluate fff there and at both endpoints.

  6. The largest of these values is the absolute maximum, and the smallest is the absolute minimum.

Example Let f(x)=x4−4x3f(x)=x^4-4x^3f(x)=x4−4x3. (a) Find and classify its critical points. (b) Find its absolute maximum and minimum on [−1,4][-1,4][−1,4].

(a) f′(x)=4x3−12x2=4x2(x−3)f'(x)=4x^3-12x^2=4x^2(x-3)f′(x)=4x3−12x2=4x2(x−3), which is zero at x=0x=0x=0 and x=3x=3x=3 and exists everywhere. With f′′(x)=12x2−24xf''(x)=12x^2-24xf′′(x)=12x2−24x, f′′(3)=108−72=36>0 ⇒ local min at (3,−27).f''(3)=108-72=36>0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local min at }(3,-27).f′′(3)=108−72=36>0 ⇒ local min at (3,−27). At x=0x=0x=0, f′′(0)=0f''(0)=0f′′(0)=0 and the test is inconclusive. The factor 4x24x^24x2 is positive on both sides of 000 and x−3x-3x−3 is negative near 000, so f′<0f'<0f′<0 on both sides: fff keeps decreasing through x=0x=0x=0. So local min at (3,−27),neither at (0,0),\boxed{\text{local min at }(3,-27)},\qquad\allowbreak \boxed{\text{neither at }(0,0)} ,local min at (3,−27)​,neither at (0,0)​, the second a horizontal point of inflection.

(b) Both critical points lie in [−1,4][-1,4][−1,4]. The values there and at the endpoints are f(−1)=5,f(0)=0,f(3)=−27,f(4)=0.f(-1)=5,\quad\allowbreak f(0)=0,\quad\allowbreak f(3)=-27,\quad\allowbreak f(4)=0 .f(−1)=5,f(0)=0,f(3)=−27,f(4)=0. So abs. max 5 at x=−1\boxed{\text{abs.\ max } 5 \text{ at } x=-1}abs. max 5 at x=−1​ and abs. min −27 at x=3\boxed{\text{abs.\ min } {-27} \text{ at } x=3}abs. min −27 at x=3​.

Check. f(x)+27=(x−3)2(x2+2x+3)f(x)+27=(x-3)^2(x^2+2x+3)f(x)+27=(x−3)2(x2+2x+3), and x2+2x+3=(x+1)2+2>0x^2+2x+3=(x+1)^2+2>0x2+2x+3=(x+1)2+2>0, so f(x)≥−27f(x)\ge-27f(x)≥−27 for every xxx, with equality only at x=3x=3x=3. And the signs used at 000: f′(−1)=−16f'(-1)=-16f′(−1)=−16 and f′(1)=−8f'(1)=-8f′(1)=−8.

Pitfalls

  • Reading f′′(0)=0f''(0)=0f′′(0)=0 as “an inflection” or “neither” without looking further: x4x^4x4 also has f′′(0)=0f''(0)=0f′′(0)=0, at a minimum. Fall back on the sign of f′f'f′.

  • Skipping the endpoints. Here the absolute maximum, 555 at x=−1x=-1x=−1, is at an endpoint, not at a critical point.

  • Dividing 4x2(x−3)=04x^2(x-3)=04x2(x−3)=0 by x2x^2x2, which loses the critical point x=0x=0x=0.

8.5 Sketching a curve by the checklist, or from a graph of f′f'f′

Problem. Sketch y=f(x)y=f(x)y=f(x) for a polynomial or a rational function, showing its intercepts, asymptotes, turning points and inflections; or describe fff from a graph of f′f'f′ alone.

Method

  1. Domain and symmetry: where fff is defined; whether it is even or odd.

  2. Intercepts: f(0)f(0)f(0), if 000 is in the domain, and the solutions of f(x)=0f(x)=0f(x)=0.

  3. Asymptotes, for a rational function: cancel any common factor of top and bottom first (a zero that cancels completely leaves a hole); then vertical where the denominator vanishes and the numerator does not; horizontal from the limits as x→±∞x\to\pm\inftyx→±∞.

  4. Increase and decrease: the sign of f′f'f′ on each interval between its zeros and the gaps in the domain. Classify the stationary points (Method 8.4).

  5. Concavity and inflections: the sign of f′′f''f′′. An inflection is a sign change of f′′f''f′′ at a point of the domain.

  6. Describe the shape in a sentence, then draw it, labelling the points you found.

Variants. From a graph of f′f'f′: fff increases where f′>0f'>0f′>0 and decreases where f′<0f'<0f′<0. A zero where f′f'f′ changes from +++ to −-− is a local maximum of fff; one where it changes from −-− to +++, a local minimum. The slope of the graph of f′f'f′ is f′′f''f′′: where that graph rises, fff is concave up, where it falls, concave down, and each turning point of f′f'f′ is an inflection of fff.

Example Find the features needed to sketch f(x)=x−1x2f(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{x^2}f(x)=x2x−1​, and describe the curve.

  • Domain and symmetry. R∖{0}\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}R∖{0}. Neither even nor odd: f(−1)=−2f(-1)=-2f(−1)=−2 but f(1)=0f(1)=0f(1)=0.

  • Intercepts. None on the yyy-axis, since 000 is not in the domain. f(x)=0f(x)=0f(x)=0 only at x=1x=1x=1.

  • Asymptotes. At x=0x=0x=0 the denominator vanishes and the numerator is −1-1−1, so x=0x=0x=0 is a vertical asymptote, with f→−∞f\to-\inftyf→−∞ on both sides since x2>0x^2>0x2>0. And f(x)=1x−1x2→0f(x)=\tfrac1x-\tfrac1{x^2}\to0f(x)=x1​−x21​→0 as x→±∞x\to\pm\inftyx→±∞, so the asymptotes are x=0 and y=0\boxed{x=0 \text{ and } y=0}x=0 and y=0​.

  • Increase/decrease. By the quotient rule, f′(x)=2−xx3f'(x)=\dfrac{2-x}{x^3}f′(x)=x32−x​. Its sign is −-−, +++, −-− on (−∞,0)(-\infty,0)(−∞,0), (0,2)(0,2)(0,2) and (2,∞)(2,\infty)(2,∞): fff decreases, increases, then decreases.

  • Classification. The only stationary point is x=2x=2x=2, where f′f'f′ changes from +++ to −-−: a local maximum at (2,14)\boxed{(2,\tfrac14)}(2,41​)​.

  • Concavity. f′′(x)=2x−6x4f''(x)=\dfrac{2x-6}{x^4}f′′(x)=x42x−6​ has the sign of x−3x-3x−3: concave down on (−∞,0)(-\infty,0)(−∞,0) and on (0,3)(0,3)(0,3), concave up on (3,∞)(3,\infty)(3,∞), with an inflection at (3,29)\boxed{(3,\tfrac29)}(3,92​)​.

The left branch starts just below y=0y=0y=0 far to the left and falls to −∞-\infty−∞ beside x=0x=0x=0. The right branch rises from −∞-\infty−∞ beside x=0x=0x=0, crosses the axis at (1,0)(1,0)(1,0), peaks at (2,14)(2,\tfrac14)(2,41​), changes its bend at (3,29)(3,\tfrac29)(3,92​) and falls back towards y=0y=0y=0, staying above it.

Check. 14−f(x)=(x−2)24x2≥0\tfrac14-f(x)=\dfrac{(x-2)^2}{4x^2}\ge041​−f(x)=4x2(x−2)2​≥0, so (2,14)(2,\tfrac14)(2,41​) is the highest point of the whole graph, as the description says. The sign of fff agrees too: negative for x<1x<1x<1, positive for x>1x>1x>1.

Pitfalls

  • Reading a sign change across an asymptote as a turning point. Here f′f'f′ changes from −-− to +++ across x=0x=0x=0, but x=0x=0x=0 is not in the domain, so it is no minimum.

  • Giving a yyy-intercept when 000 is not in the domain.

  • Putting a branch on the wrong side of the horizontal asymptote y=Ly=Ly=L. The sign of f(x)−Lf(x)-Lf(x)−L for large ∣x∣\left|x\right|∣x∣ decides it. Here L=0L=0L=0, so it is the sign of fff: below y=0y=0y=0 on the left, above on the right.

8.6 An optimisation word problem

Problem. A quantity described in words is to be made as large or as small as possible, subject to a constraint.

Method

  1. Name the quantity QQQ to be optimised and the variables it depends on. A labelled sketch helps.

  2. Use the constraint to write QQQ as a function of a single variable, and state the domain: the physically meaningful interval.

  3. Find the critical points: solve Q′=0Q'=0Q′=0, and add any interior point of the domain where Q′Q'Q′ does not exist.

  4. Identify the optimum by the second-derivative test or the sign of Q′Q'Q′. Compare it with the endpoints of a closed interval, or with the behaviour at the ends of an open one.

  5. Answer the question asked: every dimension and the optimal value, with units.

The quantity to minimise is the area AAA of card. Let the base have side xxx and the box height hhh. The base and the four sides give A=x2+4xhA=x^2+4xhA=x2+4xh. The volume x2h=500x^2h=500x2h=500 fixes h=500/x2h=500/x^2h=500/x2, so A(x)=x2+4x⋅500x2=x2+2000x,x>0.A(x)=x^2+4x\cdot\frac{500}{x^2}=x^2+\frac{2000}{x},\qquad\allowbreak x>0 .A(x)=x2+4x⋅x2500​=x2+x2000​,x>0. Then A′(x)=2x−2000x2=0 ⟹ x3=1000,x=10.A'(x)=2x-\frac{2000}{x^2}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ x^3=1000,\quad\allowbreak x=10 .A′(x)=2x−x22000​=0 ⟹ x3=1000,x=10. A′′(x)=2+4000x3>0A''(x)=2+\dfrac{4000}{x^3}>0A′′(x)=2+x34000​>0 for all x>0x>0x>0, so this is a minimum; and A→∞A\to\inftyA→∞ both as x→0+x\to0^+x→0+ and as x→∞x\to\inftyx→∞, so it is the global minimum. The height is h=500/100=5h=500/100=5h=500/100=5: 10×10×5 cm,Amin⁡=300 cm2.\boxed{10\times10\times5\ \text{cm}},\qquad\allowbreak \boxed{A_{\min}=300\ \text{cm}^2} .10×10×5 cm​,Amin​=300 cm2​.

Check. 102⋅5=50010^2\cdot5=500102⋅5=500. Neighbouring widths cost more: A(9)≈303.2A(9)\approx303.2A(9)≈303.2 and A(11)≈302.8A(11)\approx302.8A(11)≈302.8. Exactly, A(x)−300=(x−10)2(x+20)x≥0A(x)-300=\dfrac{(x-10)^2(x+20)}{x}\ge0A(x)−300=x(x−10)2(x+20)​≥0 for x>0x>0x>0.

Pitfalls

  • Counting a lid: 2x2+4xh2x^2+4xh2x2+4xh is the card for a closed box.

  • Stopping at the second-derivative test on an open domain. It shows a local minimum; the behaviour at the ends shows that it is the global one.

8.7 Newton’s method and gradient descent

Problem. Find a root of f(x)=0f(x)=0f(x)=0 to a given number of decimal places by Newton’s method; minimise fff numerically by gradient descent with a learning rate η\etaη.

Method

  1. Newton: write fff, f′f'f′ and the iteration xn+1=xn−f(xn)f′(xn)x_{n+1}=x_n-\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}xn+1​=xn​−f′(xn​)f(xn​)​ explicitly, with fff and f′f'f′ substituted.

Tabulate xnx_nxn​ and f(xn)f(x_n)f(xn​) to six decimal places. If the iterates cycle or leave the interval, halve it by the sign at its midpoint and start again there.

Stop when two iterates agree to the places asked for, and confirm the rounding by a sign change: for six places, fff changes sign between x−0.0000005x-0.0000005x−0.0000005 and x+0.0000005x+0.0000005x+0.0000005, where xxx is the answer. Pitfalls

  • Rounding xnx_nxn​ to two or three places between steps. The rounding error then swamps what the method gains; keep six places or more.

  • Stepping uphill. The update subtracts ηf′(xn)\eta f'(x_n)ηf′(xn​); adding it climbs away from the minimum.

  • Taking kkk to be the coefficient of x2x^2x2. It is f′′f''f′′: here 666, not 333, so the bound is η<13\eta<\tfrac13η<31​, not η<23\eta<\tfrac23η<32​.
